terms.definitionMarkdown: A set with vector addition and real scalar multiplication satisfying associativity and commutativity of addition, a zero vector, additive inverses, the two distributive laws, scalar associativity, and $1v=v$. This course uses real vector spaces.
A subset of a vector space that contains zero and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication, using the ambient operations.
The set of all finite linear combinations of the given vectors. It is the smallest subspace containing them.
Vectors $v_1,\ldots,v_k$ are linearly independent if $a_1v_1+\cdots+a_kv_k=0$ implies that every coefficient is zero.
A linearly independent spanning set. An ordered basis gives every vector a unique list of coordinates.
The number of vectors in any basis of a finite-dimensional vector space. The zero space has dimension zero and the empty basis.
A map $T:V\to W$ satisfying $T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$ for every pair of vectors and real scalars.
For a linear map $T:V\to W$, the subspace $\ker T=\{v\in V:T(v)=0\}$ of the domain.
For a linear map $T:V\to W$, the subspace $\operatorname{im}T=\{T(v):v\in V\}$ of the codomain.
For a linear map on a finite-dimensional domain, $\dim V=\dim\ker T+\dim\operatorname{im}T$. The latter two quantities are nullity and rank.
Relative to an ordered basis $B=(b_1,\ldots,b_n)$, the coordinate column $[v]_B$ lists the unique coefficients in $v=\sum_i c_i b_i$.
For a square real matrix, a signed volume scale. It is alternating and multilinear in the columns, equals one on the identity, is multiplicative, and is nonzero exactly when the matrix is invertible.
A nonzero vector $v$ satisfying $Av=\lambda v$. The scalar $\lambda$ is its eigenvalue. Zero is permitted as an eigenvalue, never as an eigenvector.
The subspace $E_\lambda=\ker(A-\lambda I)$, including zero. Its nonzero vectors are the eigenvectors for $\lambda$.
A factorization $A=PDP^{-1}$ with $P$ invertible and $D$ diagonal. It exists over the chosen field exactly when there is a basis of eigenvectors.
On a real vector space, a symmetric bilinear pairing $\langle u,v\rangle$ with $\langle v,v\rangle>0$ for nonzero $v$. On $\mathbb R^n$, the standard example is the dot product.
Vectors are orthogonal when their inner product is zero. A list is orthonormal when its vectors have unit length and distinct vectors are orthogonal.
The vector $p$ in a subspace $W$ such that $v-p$ is orthogonal to every vector of $W$. For an orthonormal basis $q_i$ of $W$, $p=\sum_i\langle v,q_i\rangle q_i$.
Choosing $x$ to minimize $\|Ax-b\|^2$. Minimizers satisfy $A^T(Ax-b)=0$; the coefficient vector is unique when the columns of $A$ are independent.
Every real symmetric matrix has an orthonormal basis of real eigenvectors, so $A=QDQ^T$ with $Q$ orthogonal and $D$ real diagonal.
